title: Pauri 17: countless devotions
hookLine: asankh jap: countless prayers, loves, worships and austerities; whatever pleases You is good (Japji 17)

cards: Picture a clear night. You start counting the stars, get to forty, lose your place, start again, and give up. Not because you're bad at counting, but because the thing is bigger than numbers.
There's a word for that, and Pauri 17 is built on it, line after line.

teach.b: The word is asankh. A means not; sankh means number, count. Asankh: without number, countless.
Pauri 17 is a list that keeps saying it.
Its first line in the original: asankh jap asankh bhaau. Countless are the meditations, countless the loves. Then, in paraphrase: countless worships, countless austerities.
Countless scriptures, and people reciting the Vedas. Countless yogis whose minds stay detached from the world. Countless devotees reflecting on virtue and wisdom.
Countless people who are truthful, countless who are generous. Countless warriors who face the steel. Countless silent sages, their attention held in love.
Notice what's in that list: Vedic recitation, yogis, silent sages, warriors, givers.
It gathers the devotion of many kinds of people, from many ways of life, and it doesn't rank them. Then the refrain that began yesterday: what power do I have to describe it?
Whatever pleases You is good. You are forever safe, Formless One.

That's today's line: countless, and good. The stanza isn't impressed by numbers for their own sake. However many ways people devote themselves, and they are beyond counting, the measure of good isn't the count.
It's what pleases the One. Some Sikh teachers hear a quiet freedom in that: no one has to out-pray or out-give anyone else. Each is one of the countless.

how: Pauri 17 is recited in Japji Sahib each morning; pauris 17 to 19 each repeat asankh, countless, and the repetition gives the recitation a steady, rolling rhythm.

o: a conch shell blown at worship
a prayer said a set number of times

games.q: what's inside Pauri 17 — tap the pairs.

s: Pauri 17 ranks the devotions it lists from best to worst
it gathers many kinds of devotion and simply calls them countless.
Pauri 17 ends: whatever pleases You is good
the refrain says the measure isn't the count but what pleases the One.

games.q: you've read a list of countless devotions: meditators, yogis, givers, warriors, silent sages. what does Pauri 17 conclude?
o: only one kind of devotion counts.
games.why: the refrain: what power do I have to describe it? whatever pleases You is good. You are forever safe, Formless One.

practice: Count ten breaths, one on each out-breath, and if you lose count, gently start again at one. At ten, stop counting and keep breathing, noticing that the breaths go on whether you count them or not.
Rest there, in the uncounted ones.

wordCard.voice: Asankh. A, not; sankh, number. Countless. Pauri 17 uses it for the devotions of every kind of person, and ranks none of them.

carryVoice: Your line: countless, and good. Many ways of devotion, and none of them ranked. See you tomorrow.
